editorNote: Software is leaving the hobbyist shelf for the mass market, while Summer CES machines promise another fierce autumn in home computing.
morningLine: This week in 1983: software learns the hard sell, Coleco unveils Adam, and Atari remakes its home-computer line.

lead.headline: Software's Hard Sell
lead.dek: A $1.5 billion industry learns packaging, promotion and hit-making.
body: Personal-computer software is becoming a packaged-goods business. SRI International projects 1983 revenue of $1.5 billion, after $1 billion in 1982 and $600 million in 1981, and TIME counts at least 230 producers chasing annual growth near 50 percent. The machine may command the showroom, but the programs now determine what owners can actually accomplish.

The new model has hits, stars and launch campaigns. Electronic Arts presents entertainment programs in album-like sleeves and promotes their programmers as “software artists.” Lotus spent $1 million over three months advertising 1-2-3, its $495 combination of spreadsheet, database and graphing tools, and TIME reports it has become the bestselling business program.

Distribution is scaling just as quickly. Softsel expects $70 million in 1983 revenue while moving more than 3,000 products to 1,200 outlets; it accepts fewer than eight of the 400-plus programs screened in a typical month. Software-only chain Softwaire Centre International has 26 stores, 13 more under construction, and roughly 3,300 items in each shop.

Price pressure is arriving with the wider audience. Commodore says it will release about 70 titles over the summer and sell its version of Microsoft Multiplan below $100, far under editions costing as much as $275. Buyers who once studied memory maps now confront brands, shelves and advertising claims—the unmistakable signs of a young industry becoming a consumer market.

stories.headline: Coleco's Adam Takes Aim at the Family Room
stories.dek: A complete computer, printer and fast tape system targets a price below $600.
body: The surprise of Summer CES is Coleco’s Adam, promised for fall as a complete system below $600 or as a $450 expansion for ColecoVision owners. The announced package combines a Z80A processor, 80K of RAM, a 500K proprietary high-speed cassette, detachable keyboard and daisy-wheel printer.

Coleco also promises word processing, two keypad joysticks and Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom in the box, while preserving ColecoVision cartridge compatibility. Graphics are specified at 256 by 192 pixels with 16 colors and 32 sprites. Period reporting cautions that final specifications—and the practical meaning of promised Applesoft compatibility—remain unsettled.

stories.headline: Atari Clears the Deck for Four XL Machines
stories.dek: The 400, 800 and 1200XL give way to a lower-priced compatible family.
body: Atari is discontinuing the 400, 800 and 1200XL in favor of four replacements. The 16K 600XL is listed at $199 and can expand to 64K; the 64K 800XL comes in at $299, sharpening the company’s answer to the home-computer price war.

Higher models promise communications and office features. The planned 1400XL adds a 300-baud modem and Votrax speech synthesizer, while the 1450XLD adds a double-sided, double-density disk drive. Atari Publishing also says it will produce software for Commodore and Texas Instruments machines—a striking breach in the old hardware loyalties.

stories.headline: Programs May Soon Travel by Telephone
stories.dek: Retail experiments test electronic delivery without a disk on the shelf.
body: Tymshare is testing in-store electronic software delivery at four shops in the San Francisco area, TIME reports. Control Video plans to begin delivering game programs by telephone later in June.

The experiments remain small, but their logic is powerful: a retailer could offer a broader catalog without stocking every box and disk. For an industry struggling with duplication, inventory and thousands of new titles, the telephone line may become part of the software aisle.
